edges.description: The inferred step from cardiomyocyte glycogen depletion to hypertrophic remodeling of the myocardium. This edge, not the nodes on either side of it, is the contested claim in the cardiac arm: it rests on the co-occurrence of glycogen deficiency and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in the index family, it is contradicted by adult patients with the same enzymatic lesion and no cardiac involvement, and it has no supporting model system.
The remodeling is expressed clinically as hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
The cardiac substrate underlies sudden cardiac arrest, which has been the presenting event in childhood.
Glycogen synthase and glycogen are undetectable in both cardiac and skeletal muscle, reproducing the defining substrate lesion of the human disease in the same two tissues.
edges.target: Muscle and Cardiac Glycogen Store Depletion

edges.description: The mouse does not reproduce the human cardiac lesion. Its cardiac pathology is a developmental malformation that kills most nulls around birth; the survivors show normal cardiac morphology and function rather than the hypertrophic remodeling seen in surviving human patients.
edges.limitations: The murine cardiac phenotype is developmental (defects beginning 11.5-14.5 dpc, about 90% perinatal lethality) and is therefore a different lesion from the postnatal hypertrophic cardiomyopathy of human GSD0B. The surviving minority are, by selection, those without a cardiac defect, so the model provides no surviving-animal readout of the human hypertrophic phenotype and cannot be used to study its natural history or to test interventions against it.

nodes.description: Cardiomyocytes are left without the glycogen reserve they draw on when workload rises, which is why the reported cardiac events are exertional. The node covers the cellular energetic deficit only; whether it goes on to produce hypertrophic remodeling is a separate, contested step recorded on the downstream edge.

nodes.description: Muscle deprived of glycogen reweights toward oxidative metabolism. On biopsy this appears as a predominance of oxidative fibres with mitochondrial proliferation, and molecularly as a shift away from the glycogenolytic and glycolytic route. The compensation is florid enough to be mistaken for primary mitochondrial disease: in one fatal childhood case the post-mortem was initially read as mitochondrial myopathy before the mitochondrial changes were recognized as compensatory.

nodes.description: Biallelic loss-of-function GYS1 variants abolish or severely reduce muscle glycogen synthase, the enzyme that elongates the glycogen chain by transferring glucose from UDP-glucose. Reported lesions include a homozygous nonsense variant, canonical splice-donor variants that mis-splice exon 4, and a missense variant, and the biochemical consequence has been measured directly as reduced enzyme activity and reduced protein.

nodes.description: Constitutive disruption of Gys1 removes glycogen from muscle, heart and several other tissues. The model is informative for the substrate lesion, but its cardiac course diverges sharply from the human disease: about 90% of nulls die perinatally from a developmental cardiac defect arising between 11.5 and 14.5 dpc, while the roughly 10% that survive have hearts of normal morphology and function - the opposite of the human phenotype, where survivors are the ones who develop hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in childhood.
